@graph.headline: The SDIRA Digital Asset Value Attestation: Annual Custodian Requirements, IRS Compliance Expectations, and When a Qualified Appraisal Is the Defensible Standard
@graph.description: Every self-directed IRA holding digital assets must report a fair market value each year. This practitioner-level guide explains the Form 5498 attestation cycle, who is legally permitted to value IRA digital assets, the prohibited-transaction traps, and when a USPAP-compliant qualified appraisal is the only defensible standard.

about.name: SDIRA Digital Asset Value Attestation
about.description: A practitioner-level guide to the annual fair market value attestation required for digital assets held in self-directed IRAs: Form 5498 reporting mechanics, the December 31 valuation date, the Cartwright fair market value standard, GAO-17-02's finding of no IRS valuation guidance for unconventional assets, who is legally permitted to value SDIRA digital assets (independent qualified appraisers, not custodians or disqualified persons under IRC Section 4975), the evidence spectrum from liquid crypto to illiquid NFTs and DeFi positions, why exchange screenshots and NFT floor prices are not defensible fair market value, prohibited-transaction traps including private key custody and personal receipt of staking or lending rewards, the SECURE 2.0 RMD age and penalty framework (25 percent excise tax reduced to 10 percent if corrected timely), Form 1099-R exposure on undocumented write-offs, when a USPAP-compliant qualified appraisal is required versus a reasonable documented estimate, and the practical Q3-to-February attestation calendar for holders, CPAs, and attorneys.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a qualified appraisal every year for crypto in my SDIRA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. For deeply liquid assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, custodians and the IRS generally accept a documented, reasonable valuation — a date-stamped price record from a reputable source as of the December 31 valuation date. A qualified appraisal becomes the standard when the account holds illiquid or complex digital assets (NFTs, DeFi positions, locked or thinly traded tokens), when a taxable event like a Roth conversion or in-kind distribution is involved, when custodian policy requires it, or when the position is material to your financial picture.

mainEntity.name: Can I use an exchange screenshot for the year-end value of my SDIRA crypto?

acceptedAnswer.text: For Tier 1 assets, a date-stamped price record from a reputable, named venue is reasonable support. For NFTs, DeFi positions, and other illiquid assets, a screenshot is not a defensible valuation: it is self-selected, unverified, potentially wash-trade-inflated, and carries no professional accountability. An NFT's floor price, in particular, is not its fair market value under the standard adopted in United States v. Cartwright.

mainEntity.name: Who is allowed to perform the annual valuation of SDIRA digital assets?

acceptedAnswer.text: The valuation must come from a competent, independent third party. The IRA owner, the owner's family, entities the owner controls, and other disqualified persons under IRC Section 4975 cannot perform the valuation. Custodians do not value alternative assets — they report the documentation the owner supplies. A USPAP-compliant qualified appraiser with verifiable digital asset experience satisfies the independence and competence requirements.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my SDIRA custodian does not receive a year-end value?

acceptedAnswer.text: The custodian must still file Form 5498, and it cannot report a value it does not have. Consequences vary by custodian and account agreement but commonly include compliance holds, accelerated deadlines, and in some cases forced liquidation provisions. Inaccurate or missing valuations are among the most commonly cited Form 5498 errors — and the exposure belongs to the account owner.

mainEntity.name: Can an IRA owner hold the private keys to crypto inside a self-directed IRA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Generally, no — not without serious risk. Personal control of the keys can support a deemed-distribution theory (the assets were available to the owner) and a prohibited-transaction theory (use of plan assets for personal benefit) under Section 4975. Legitimate arrangements hold keys in a custodian-controlled wallet or as an asset of an IRA-LLC managed under plan rules. If a platform gave you the keys and called the account self-directed, obtain immediate professional review.

mainEntity.name: What value does the IRS use to calculate RMDs from a crypto IRA?

acceptedAnswer.text: RMDs are calculated using the prior year-end (December 31) fair market value of the account divided by the life-expectancy factor from the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table — the same value reported on Form 5498. An understated year-end attestation therefore mechanically produces an understated RMD and, under SECURE 2.0, exposure to the 25 percent excise tax (reduced to 10 percent if corrected timely).

mainEntity.name: Is staking or lending digital assets inside my SDIRA a prohibited transaction?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no prohibited-transaction rule unique to digital assets, and staking or lending is not prohibited in itself. The analysis turns on who controls the asset and who receives the rewards. Rewards that accrue to the account are plan income; rewards that flow to the owner personally, or to a wallet the owner controls outside the plan, can constitute use of plan assets for personal benefit under Section 4975.

mainEntity.name: What documentation should I keep for my SDIRA's digital asset valuation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Maintain the account inventory, wallet and contract addresses, purchase and transfer records, staking or lending agreements, the custodian's valuation form and documentation policy, date-stamped price evidence for liquid positions, and the full appraisal report for any professionally valued position. Retain the complete file permanently — the IRS can examine a valuation years after the custodian's portal purges the data.
